cls: Halogenated 8-hydroxyquinoline anti-infectives (intestinal amebicide / topical antiseptic-antifungal-antibacterial group)
pharm: Metal-chelating halogenated 8-hydroxyquinolines with broad antibacterial, antifungal and antiprotozoal activity, acting locally in the gut or on the skin by binding essential metal ions required for microbial enzymes.
quick: Topical creams 1-3% applied 2-3 times daily; oral diiodohydroxyquinoline (where available) 630-650 mg three times daily x20 days for amebiasis
Oral doses with/after food; topicals applied to skin
Avoid - particularly oral use; topical use only if clearly needed
Avoid oral use; topical with caution
Caution; iodine-containing agents affect thyroid/iodine handling
Neurologic status (oral clioquinol), thyroid function tests (iodinated agents), local skin reactions
summary: This is a GROUP entry for the halogenated 8-hydroxyquinolines - including clioquinol (iodochlorhydroxyquin), chlorquinaldol, and diiodohydroxyquinoline (iodoquinol) - a class of metal-chelating anti-infectives with antibacterial, antifungal and antiprotozoal activity. They are used mainly TOPICALLY (creams, ointments, ear/skin preparations, often combined with a corticosteroid) for infected eczema, dermatoses and superficial bacterial/fungal skin and ear infections, and ORALLY (diiodohydroxyquinoline/iodoquinol where still marketed) as a luminal amebicide for intestinal amebiasis and for Dientamoeba/Balantidium infections. Oral clioquinol was widely withdrawn after it was linked to subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON), a serious neurotoxic syndrome reported especially in Japan, so oral hydroxyquinolines are largely restricted or unavailable and these agents are NOT FDA-approved for oral systemic use in the United States. Iodine-containing members (iodoquinol, clioquinol) can interfere with thyroid function tests and should be used cautiously in thyroid disease. Information here is drawn from European/UK sources (SmPC/BNF) and the WHO/historical literature rather than an FDA label.
indications: Topical treatment of infected or secondarily infected dermatoses and eczema, and superficial bacterial/fungal skin and outer-ear infections (often combined with a corticosteroid)
Oral luminal (intraluminal) treatment of intestinal amebiasis as a contact amebicide (diiodohydroxyquinoline/iodoquinol, where available)
Treatment of Dientamoeba fragilis and Balantidium coli intestinal infections (iodoquinol)

dosage.d: Apply a 1-3% cream/ointment (alone or with a corticosteroid) to the affected area
dosage.n: Short courses; avoid large denuded areas or occlusion (systemic iodine absorption)

dosage.d: 630-650 mg three times daily for 20 days
dosage.n: Luminal agent - combine with a tissue amebicide (e.g., metronidazole) for invasive disease

dosage.d: Approximately 30-40 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses (max 1.95 g/day) for 20 days
dosage.n: Per weight; limit duration and total dose to reduce neuro-ocular toxicity

admin: Prefer short-duration topical use; avoid application to extensive raw/denuded surfaces or under occlusion to limit systemic iodine absorption
For oral amebiasis, give after meals to reduce gastric irritation and complete the prescribed course (typically 20 days) without exceeding recommended dose/duration
Use a luminal agent like iodoquinol together with a systemic tissue amebicide (e.g., metronidazole) when treating invasive amebic disease
Avoid prolonged or high-dose oral use, which has been associated with serious neuro-ocular toxicity (SMON, optic neuropathy)
Be aware that iodine-containing members interfere with thyroid-function tests for weeks - check thyroid status where relevant
Note that these preparations can stain skin, hair and fabric
moa: Halogenated 8-hydroxyquinolines are chelating agents: the 8-hydroxyquinoline nucleus binds divalent and trivalent metal ions (such as iron, copper, zinc, manganese) that are cofactors for essential microbial metalloenzymes. By sequestering these metals - or, in some settings, acting as ionophores that disrupt intracellular metal homeostasis - they inhibit the growth of bacteria, fungi and protozoa. As luminal amebicides they act by direct contact within the gut lumen against the trophozoite/cyst forms of Entamoeba histolytica rather than against tissue-invasive organisms, which is why they are paired with a systemic agent for invasive disease.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to hydroxyquinolines, iodine or quinoline derivatives
Significant optic neuropathy or pre-existing neuropathy (oral use)
relative: Thyroid disease (iodine-containing agents alter thyroid function and tests)
Prolonged or high-dose oral therapy (cumulative neurotoxicity risk)
Application to large areas of broken skin or under occlusion (systemic absorption)
monitor: Neurologic and visual symptoms with oral therapy (peripheral neuropathy, optic neuropathy)
Local skin reactions/sensitization with topical use
Stool examination for clearance in amebiasis

preg: Hydroxyquinolines, especially oral iodine-containing agents, should be avoided in pregnancy; absorbed iodine can affect the fetal thyroid, and safety is not established. Use topical preparations during pregnancy only if clearly needed and over limited areas.
lact: Oral use should be avoided during breastfeeding because absorbed iodine can affect the infant's thyroid; topical use should be limited and not applied to the breast/nipple area.
renal: There is limited specific information; use with caution in renal impairment, particularly with systemic absorption of iodinated agents.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; iodine-containing agents and any systemic absorption warrant caution, and prolonged systemic exposure has been associated with toxicity.

moderate: Other neurotoxic drugs - potential additive neurotoxicity with oral hydroxyquinolines
Iodine-containing drugs/contrast and antithyroid drugs - additive effects on thyroid/iodine status
minor: May chelate co-administered metal ions/cations, theoretically reducing absorption of certain mineral supplements
interactions.food: Take oral doses with or after food to reduce gastric irritation.
interactions.diagnostics: Iodine-containing members can markedly elevate protein-bound iodine and interfere with thyroid-function tests for weeks; can cause false results in tests dependent on iodine.

common: Local skin irritation, stinging or contact sensitization (topical)
Staining of skin, hair and clothing
Gastrointestinal upset - nausea, diarrhea, abdominal cramps (oral)
serious: Subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON) - peripheral neuropathy with optic atrophy/visual loss (historically with oral clioquinol)
emergency: Acute visual loss or rapidly progressive neuropathy (stop the drug and seek urgent care)

monitoring: Neurologic and visual function during oral therapy (watch for neuropathy and optic symptoms)
Thyroid-function tests when using iodine-containing agents, especially with prolonged use
Local tolerance and sensitization with topical preparations
Stool clearance of parasites after a course of amebiasis treatment
counsel: Use these preparations exactly as directed and for the shortest course needed
For skin/ear creams, apply a thin layer to the affected area only; they can stain skin, hair and clothing
If taking the tablets for an intestinal infection, finish the full course and take them after food
Stop the medicine and seek urgent advice if you notice changes in your vision, numbness, tingling, or weakness in the legs
Tell your doctor if you have thyroid problems - iodine-containing forms can affect thyroid tests
Avoid prolonged or repeated oral courses unless your doctor specifically advises it
pk: Topical effect local and prompt; oral luminal amebicidal action within the gut over the treatment course
Limited/variable systemic absorption from gut and skin
Variable; iodine from iodinated agents persists in the body for weeks
Topical effect during application; oral amebicide course typically 20 days
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture, per product label
pearls: GROUP ENTRY for halogenated 8-hydroxyquinolines (clioquinol, chlorquinaldol, diiodohydroxyquinoline/iodoquinol) - NOT FDA-approved for oral systemic use; information here is from European/UK (SmPC/BNF) and WHO/historical sources
Oral clioquinol was withdrawn after being linked to subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON) - avoid prolonged/high-dose oral use and watch for visual and neurologic symptoms
Mainly used TOPICALLY for infected dermatoses/skin and ear infections (often with a corticosteroid); iodoquinol is an oral LUMINAL amebicide
Luminal amebicides act only in the gut lumen - combine with a tissue amebicide (e.g., metronidazole) for invasive amebiasis
Iodine-containing members interfere with thyroid-function tests for weeks and can affect thyroid function - use caution in thyroid disease
These agents chelate metals (the basis of their broad antimicrobial action) and can stain skin, hair and fabric
missed: If an oral dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose, then skip it; do not double up, and complete the full course. For topical use, apply the missed dose when remembered.
overdose: Overdose, particularly with prolonged oral use, can cause serious neuro-ocular toxicity (peripheral neuropathy and optic neuropathy) and, with iodinated agents, iodine toxicity and thyroid disturbance. There is no specific antidote; discontinue the drug immediately and provide supportive care, with neurologic and ophthalmologic assessment and management of any thyroid effects.
